messages.subject: One student proposal per project?
parts:
Dear all,

I am very new in the Google Summer of Code (first-time mentor, and never
been a student in GSoC), and none of the other mentors on my project have
prior experience either. Please forgive my question if it's obvious, I
couldn't find a clear answer in the different manuals and FAQS.

I understand that it is my job (mostly based on the tests and interactions
with students) to select one student prior to application. Then the student
can draft a proposal on GSoC website, which is then opened to comments
before the final version that will be applied (deadline next Friday).

Is this all correct? In the case of several students showing interest, it
is really my decision to select one, or can several proposals (i.e. several
students) apply to the same project?

Thanks for the answer to this question, which is rather critical at this
stage. And sorry for asking so late...

Best,
Mathieu.



--

Mathieu Basille

messages.subject: Re: One student proposal per project?
parts:
On 03/19/2016 10:28 AM, Mathieu Basille wrote:
> I am very new in the Google Summer of Code (first-time mentor, and never
> been a student in GSoC), and none of the other mentors on my project have
> prior experience either. Please forgive my question if it's obvious, I
> couldn't find a clear answer in the different manuals and FAQS.
>
> I understand that it is my job (mostly based on the tests and interactions
> with students) to select one student prior to application. Then the student
> can draft a proposal on GSoC website, which is then opened to comments
> before the final version that will be applied (deadline next Friday).
>
> Is this all correct? In the case of several students showing interest, it
> is really my decision to select one, or can several proposals (i.e. several
> students) apply to the same project?
>
> Thanks for the answer to this question, which is rather critical at this
> stage. And sorry for asking so late...

It is up to the organization administrators how many slots you request,
and once you get the slots, how you choose to allocate them.

If you are a new organization and new mentors, it is likely, based on
prior experience, that Google will not award you very many slots.

In our organization, we have a mix of 'open' applications, where no
student has been identified before the beginning of the GSoC application
period, and 'strong student' projects, where a strong student has been
working together with mentors potentially for months before GSoC preparing.

None of the above matters when it is time to award slots though... the
only things we consider then are the strength of the application and the
plan, and the commitment of all parties: student and mentors (we require
at least two mentors per student project, one of whom must typically
have prior GSoC experience).

Several students can apply to the same project idea. You'll have to
choose applicants based on the strength of their application and the
number of slots you are awarded.

Regards,

Brian


--
Brian G. Peterson

parts:
Thank you Brian for your very fast answer. So I definitely fall in the first category ("'open' applications, where no student has been identified before the beginning of the GSoC application period"). We are three mentors in the project (I forgot to mention that), unfortunately with no prior GSoC experience, and several students expressed interest and are at various stages of the test or developing their application.

The one thing I don't understand is that I thought that 1 idea = 1 slot = 1 student. Am I understand it correctly? If this is the case, I only expect 1 slot maximum. Is it fine to let several students apply to this project independently? Or is it better to let one of them develop the best application right away? (in order to not have others work too hard for something they won't get)

Thank you very much for your guidance. Indeed, having a mentor with prior GSoC experience would have been a real plus... I'm the one to blame on that since I heard of this year opening very late (just a couple of weeks ago).

Mathieu.

messages.author: b98e21751c27e8b9
messages.subject: Re: One student proposal per project?
parts:
Matthieu,

I wanted to apologize that in my hurry to answer your query I didn't
notice that this was on the R GSoC list and not the main GSoC mentors
list with participants from all organizations participating in GSoC.
I'll answer with more specificity to R. This is a long email, but I
recommend all R mentors and aspiring students read it.

Specific to how R runs this process, we require strong applications from
any student who wants a slot.

For any student wishing to participate in GSoC, it is a competition for
limited slots, so they should be working hard to write the best
application that they can. It is fine, and expected, that multiple
students will apply to exciting project ideas. In the past, we have
had as many as 9 applications for a single project (the student who
submitted the best application for that project is now an R GSoC
mentor). We've tried to provide some guidance for students and mentors
on what is included in a good application in the template here:
https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2016/wiki/application-template

For you and your co-mentors, this means encouraging the students who
have submitted test results to get working on their applications and get
a draft application posted as soon as possible. Once a student has
posted a draft application, you and your co-mentors should be asking
questions which would help the student strengthen their application and
give you (and the student) more confidence that they can complete a high
quality project over the summer. Students who are 'radio silent' during
this early comments phase are a red flag, and historically will not have
high chances of success.

Assuming we get to the end of next week and you have multiple strong
proposals for your project, you and your co-mentors will need to confer
privately and discuss which is the strongest of the applications you've
received, and which one project you would ideally like to mentor. In
rare cases when there have been multiple strong applicants for a
project, experienced mentors, and the top applications focused on
sufficiently different aspects of the project idea, R has split a
project into two and awarded two slots. We do this reluctantly, and
only with experienced mentors.

For mentors new to GSoC, one of the things I've observed is that new
mentors consistently underestimate how much time they will spend on GSoC
over the course of the summer. From Google's data, the average amount
of time a mentor spends on GSoC is 10-15hrs per week. New mentors, or
mentors with projects that require a good deal of domain or technical
expertise, often find themselves spending even more than this helping
their students during the summer to get a successful outcome.

For your postGIS project proposal, the email addresses of your
co-mentors need to be added to the project idea page (and/or
communicated directly to me off-list) so that I can invite them to the
Google system for administering GSoC this year.

The process around next Friday's application deadline is that Toby,
Virgilio and I will start discussing mid next week the number of strong
applications that we see for R GSoC projects. (Students, this is why
your draft applications should be submitted ASAP and refined in concert
with your mentors over the next five days) At some point (I need to
check the schedule and the new admin system) we will need to request
slots from Google. Sometime after the student application period
closes, Google will tell us how many slots we receive.

Toby, Virgilio, and I will privately solicit input from mentors who have
multiple strong proposals, but ultimately we need to assign students to
slots. Google (not us, and not our mentors) will announce to students
whether their applications have been accepted or rejected on Apr 22.

Regards,

Brian

parts:
Thank you Brian for your very detailed answer! No need to apologize, most
of my comments/questions come from the absence of experienced mentors for
my projects... and the very bad idea of doing it a bit last minute.

Your answer is perfect: very clear and removed all my doubts. I am ready to
spend that time on the project, if a good application is selected for it
(and this is true too for the other mentors). This is a project that is
really important to us, only we cannot work full time on it. Summertime is
the perfect timing to mentor a student on it, hopefully we'll get good
applications.

I just added the email addresses for the other two mentors on the wiki. I
will send you a private email shortly just in case. Thanks for the reminder
that ALL mentors need to be invited!

Best,
Mathieu.
